sobre.title: Art always called to me. One day, I answered.
sobre.text:
For a long time I thought art was not a possible path for me. Until I put fear aside and made my first drawings. Oil pastel was my first passion; then came watercolor, courses and plenty of experimenting with materials.

Today I paint landscapes, memories and small moments, inspired by Monet, Degas and Van Gogh, and I bring this passion to digital planners too.

seo.title: About Mariane Nunes | Efúgio Atelier
seo.description: The story of Mariane Nunes, a watercolor and oil pastel artist who one day decided to answer the call of art.

sobre.title: Art always called to me. One day, I answered.

children.text: My name is Mariane and, for as long as I can remember, art has held a deep fascination for me. I could spend hours watching artists turn a blank sheet into something capable of awakening feelings, memories and new ways of seeing the world.

For a long time, though, I believed art was not a possible path for me. For almost 30 years, I admired paintings and drawings from a distance, convinced I did not have enough talent to create. I was enchanted by the process, but I did not allow myself to try.

Until, at 30, I decided to put fear aside and make my first drawings and paintings. It was in oil pastel that I found my first great passion: its intense colors, its texture and the freedom to create without chasing perfect shapes awakened something that had always been inside me.

Then came watercolor and acrylic paint. I studied techniques, took courses, experimented with materials and tried to understand better not only how to paint, but how to find my own way of expressing myself.

Today, I feel the time has come to share with the world everything I have been building. My work focuses mainly on watercolor and oil pastel. I like to portray natural landscapes, and I find inspiration in the movement, light and color of Impressionist artists such as Monet, Degas and Van Gogh. I also explore abstract and modern art, allowing each work to find its own path.
This passion has also become digital products: planners inspired by great painters, so that art can be part of the routine of anyone who plans their own days.

For me, art goes far beyond realism. I do not paint only what I see: I paint what I feel. I try to create freely, without holding on to perfect forms, turning colors, landscapes and emotions into records of a moment.
My story with art is also a story about new beginnings. About realizing that it is never too late to try, to learn and to make room for what has always called to us from within.

children.text: This page explains, in simple terms, how the Efúgio Atelier website handles the information provided by visitors.
What data is collected
The site only collects the information you fill in on the contact and newsletter forms: name, email, subject, the work or product you are interested in and your message.
How the data is used
The contact form opens your email app with the message already filled in, addressed to
mawebcontent@gmail.com
. The data does not pass through any server of the site itself.
The email entered in the newsletter is used only to send news about Efúgio Atelier works, products and launches.
Purchases on Etsy
Digital products are sold through Etsy. When you click "Buy on Etsy," you go to the Etsy website, and your purchase data follows Etsy's own privacy policy.
Sharing
No personal data is sold or shared with third parties for advertising purposes.
Your rights
You can ask at any time for your email to be removed from the newsletter or for clarification about how your data is used by writing to
mawebcontent@gmail.com
Cookies

Besides the cookies needed for the site's basic operation, this site uses Google Tag Manager to load Google's measurement and marketing tools, such as Google Analytics, which help us understand, in aggregate, how the pages are visited. These tools only use cookies if you accept them in the cookie notice. You can change your choice at any time under Cookie preferences, in the site footer, and you can also delete or block cookies in your browser settings.

children.text: Daily, weekly and monthly pages of the
En Plein Air
planner.

A digital planner is a planner in file form, usually a PDF, that you open in a note-taking app and fill in with a digital pen or the keyboard. It brings together the pages of a paper planner, such as a monthly calendar, weekly planning and lists, with one advantage: clickable tabs and links that take you straight to each section.
If you have never used one, this guide explains how a digital planner works, what you need to get started, how to organize your month, week and day, and how it differs from a paper planner.
A digital planner is a PDF with planning pages and internal links, used in note-taking apps.
To start, you need the file, an app that opens PDFs with links and, ideally, a tablet with a pen.
Undated planners can start in any month and be used in any year.
What keeps the habit going is a short review ritual, not filling in every page.
How a digital planner works

In practice, a digital planner is a document with dozens of pages organized by section. What sets it apart from an ordinary PDF are the hyperlinks: when you tap a tab, such as "month," "week" or "notes," you go straight to that page, without scrolling through the whole file.

You write on the pages with your note-taking app's tools, such as pen, highlighter and eraser. Since everything stays in the file, you can erase without leaving marks, move a task to another day and keep the planner tidy.

Some planners come with extra features. In the Efúgio Atelier planners, for example, besides the clickable tabs, there are links to create events in Google Calendar and in Apple's calendar, which helps turn a written appointment into a reminder.
Undated digital planners

Undated planners have month, week and day pages without the dates filled in. You write the dates yourself and can start at any time of year, without wasting pages for months that have already passed. The
Luminous Days
and
En Plein Air
planners are undated, for use in any year.
What you need to get started
The planner file
, usually a PDF.
A note-taking app that opens PDFs with links.
The pages of the Efúgio Atelier planners mention, for example, Goodnotes, Notability, Noteshelf and Xodo. Before buying, check that the app you plan to use is available for your device.
A tablet with a digital pen
, which is the most comfortable way to use a digital planner on a tablet, because it lets you write by hand.
A printer, if you prefer paper.
Some planners can also be printed. En Plein Air, for example, is a PDF to use on a tablet or print.
Step by step: how to use a digital planner
Download the file.

For planners sold on Etsy, the download is done through the Etsy website, in your phone's or computer's browser, in the purchases area of your account. According to the guide that comes with the Efúgio Atelier planners, digital purchases cannot be downloaded through the Etsy app; you can also use the link in the receipt email.
Open the PDF in your note-taking app.
Usually you just open the file and choose the app, or use the import option inside the app itself.
Explore the tabs.
Before writing, tap each tab to understand how the planner is organized.
Duplicate the pages you will use most.
In an undated planner, you can duplicate week or notes pages whenever you need to.
Fill in the first month.
Start with the current month: note important dates, fixed appointments and goals.
Use the calendar links.
Create events and reminders for the appointments you cannot forget.
Download guide that comes with the Efúgio Atelier planners.
How to organize your routine with a digital planner
Organizing with a digital planner works best when each type of page has a clear job. A simple way to divide them:
Month: the overview
Use the monthly page for what is fixed and important: birthdays, bills, trips, deadlines and two or three goals for the month. It is the map and does not need details.
Week: the real planning

The weekly page is where the month turns into action. Spread your tasks across the days, taking into account the appointments you already have, and choose the week's priorities. A good time for this is the weekend or the first morning of the week.
Day: focus and adjustments
The daily page is for the busiest days: list the three most important tasks, the times and what needs to be remembered. On quiet days, the weekly page may be enough.
Daily, weekly and monthly pages of the
Luminous Days
planner.
Lists, logs and the things that do you good

Besides the calendar, many planners include pages for goals, to-do lists and logs. En Plein Air, for example, has goals, priorities, to-do lists and a mood and energy tracker, and both Efúgio Atelier planners include reading and movie journals. These pages make the planner a place to keep track of what inspires you too, not just your obligations.
Digital planner or paper planner?
Both work, and the best choice depends on how you like to get organized. An honest comparison:

cells.text: On your tablet, alongside other files
In a physical notebook, to carry in your bag
Erases without leaving marks and lets you move content
You can duplicate the ones you use most
Can have links to create calendar events
On screen, with a digital pen
A charged device and a note-taking app
Just the notebook and a pen

children.text: If you like the feel of paper but want the flexibility of digital, one option is to print just a few pages, as long as the planner allows it.
Tips for sticking with your planner
Keep the planner within reach.
If it is on the tablet you use every day, it is easier to open.
Treat the planner as an ally, not an obligation.
It does not need to be pretty or complete to work.
Do a quick review at the end of the day.
Five minutes to see what got done and note down the next day creates a rhythm.
Start with a few sections.
Use month and week for a few weeks before adding lists and logs.
Personalize it little by little.
Colors, markings and digital stickers make the planner feel like yours. En Plein Air, for example, comes with a bonus sheet of digital stickers.
Art in your routine: the Efúgio Atelier planners
The Efúgio Atelier digital planners bring together organization and art history:
Luminous Days
, inspired by Van Gogh: 71 undated pages, with daily, weekly and monthly planning, reading and movie journals and six guided encounters with the painter's works. File in English.
En Plein Air
, inspired by Impressionist painting: 76 undated pages, in English, Spanish and Portuguese, with planning, goals, a mood tracker, artwork observation pages and a sheet of digital stickers.
To learn about the references behind them, read also
what Impressionism is
Start with next week

You do not need to plan the whole year today. Open the planner, fill in the current month and organize next week. If this routine of a few minutes holds for a month, the planner will have done its job.

children.text: Claude Monet,
The Cliff Walk at Pourville
, 1882. Oil on canvas. The Art Institute of Chicago, Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Larned Coburn Memorial Collection (public domain).

Impressionism was an art movement that emerged in France in the 1870s, when a group of painters decided to exhibit on their own, outside the official Paris Salon. Instead of smoothly finished historical scenes, these artists painted the light of a moment, modern life and landscapes observed outdoors, with vivid colors and loose, visible brushstrokes.

This guide walks through the history of Impressionism from the first exhibition, explains where the name came from, what the characteristics of Impressionism are, who the main Impressionist painters were and why Vincent van Gogh, though closely tied to this story, is considered a Post-Impressionist.
When:
the group's first exhibition opened on April 15, 1874, in Paris. There were eight exhibitions in all, the last in 1886.
What it sought:
to capture the light, color and atmosphere of a moment, with loose brushstrokes and pure colors.
Who:
Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Berthe Morisot, Camille Pissarro, Alfred Sisley, Mary Cassatt and Gustave Caillebotte, among others.
And Van Gogh?
He was influenced by Impressionism in Paris, but he belongs to Post-Impressionism.
How Impressionism began

In 19th-century France, the main showcase for a painter was the Salon, the great official exhibition in Paris. Being accepted or rejected by its jury could make or break a career, and official taste favored subjects considered noble and meticulously finished paintings.

To avoid depending on that system, a group of artists founded an independent society, the Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors, Printmakers, etc., and organized their own show. It opened on April 15, 1874, in the former studio of the photographer Nadar, on the Boulevard des Capucines, bringing together more than 30 artists. Among them were Monet, Renoir, Degas, Morisot, Pissarro, Sisley and Cézanne.

The exhibition was not a manifesto of style. According to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, what united the participants was above all their independence from the Salon. After 1874 the group held seven more exhibitions, until 1886. Camille Pissarro was the only one to take part in all of them, and Berthe Morisot was in seven.
Where the name "Impressionism" comes from
One of the canvases Claude Monet showed in 1874 depicted the port of Le Havre at dawn, among mist, cranes and masts, with an orange sun reflected in the water. Painted in 1872, the picture was titled
Impression, Sunrise
Impression, soleil levant
). According to the Musée Marmottan Monet, which holds the work, Monet chose that name because the canvas could not pass for a simple view of Le Havre.
The critic Louis Leroy seized on the title to mock the group in an article published on April 25, 1874, in the satirical newspaper
Le Charivari

, called "The Exhibition of the Impressionists." To him, those paintings looked like sketches, not finished works. The word, born as a jibe, was later used in a positive sense by other critics, such as Jules Castagnary, and ended up naming the movement.
Characteristics of Impressionism
More than a formula, Impressionism was a new way of looking. Some characteristics appear often in the movement's works.
Light as the subject

The Impressionists wanted to record how light transforms a scene at a specific moment of the day. Shadows and reflections came to be painted with colors instead of neutral grays and blacks. A shadow on snow could be blue; a reflection on water, orange and violet.
Loose, visible brushstrokes

Instead of hiding the work of the brush, the Impressionists used short, broken brushstrokes, with pure colors placed side by side. Up close, the surface looks like a set of patches; a few steps away, the scene comes together. Despite their spontaneous look, many compositions were carefully planned.
Vivid colors

New synthetic pigments expanded the painters' palette. Together with the absence of the golden varnish common at the time, these colors made Impressionist canvases shocking to a public used to the more sober tones of academic painting.
Scenes of modern life

The subjects changed too. Out went the great historical and mythological scenes, and in came leisure in the countryside and the suburbs, trains and factories in the landscape, the newly rebuilt Paris, cafés, concerts and dances.
Painting outdoors
Many Impressionists painted directly in front of their subject, outdoors, or
en plein air

, to observe real light. The practice existed before them, but it gained strength in this period. It is often said that the metal paint tube, patented by the American painter John Goffe Rand in the early 1840s, made working outside the studio easier. Historians point out, however, that portable easels and paint boxes also played an important role.
Claude Monet,
Springtime

, 1872. Oil on canvas. The Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (public domain). Camille, the painter's wife, reads in the shade of the trees, and the light coming through the leaves appears as patches on her dress and on the grass.
Academic painting and Impressionism: the main differences

cells.text: Historical, mythological and religious scenes, formal portraits
Landscapes, the modern city, leisure and everyday life
Colored shadows and pure colors side by side
Often outdoors, in front of the subject
To record the perception of a moment

children.text: The main Impressionist painters
Claude Monet (1840–1926).
The name most associated with the movement. He returned to the same subject at different times of day and in different seasons to study light, as in the series of haystacks and water lilies.
Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1841–1919).
Scenes of leisure, parties and portraits full of light, such as
Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette
Edgar Degas (1834–1917).
Dancers, horse races and backstage scenes, with unexpected framing. He also worked extensively in pastel.
Berthe Morisot (1841–1895).
Intimate, domestic scenes painted with very light brushstrokes. She took part in the first exhibition, in 1874, with
The Cradle
Camille Pissarro (1830–1903).
Rural landscapes and city views. He was the only one to exhibit in all eight of the group's shows.
Alfred Sisley (1839–1899).
Rivers, skies and villages around Paris.
Mary Cassatt (1844–1926).
An American based in Paris, known for her scenes of mothers and children.
Gustave Caillebotte (1848–1894).
A painter and collector who supported the group, author of
Paris Street; Rainy Day
Édouard Manet, often associated with the group, was an important reference for these painters, but he did not take part in the Impressionist exhibitions.
Impressionism and Post-Impressionism: where Van Gogh fits in

Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) often appears in lists of Impressionist painters, but, historically speaking, he belongs to Post-Impressionism. The term was coined by the English critic Roger Fry in 1910, when he organized the exhibition
Manet and the Post-Impressionists
. According to Tate, it usually refers to four main names: Paul Cézanne, Paul Gauguin, Georges Seurat and Van Gogh.

These artists started from the achievements of Impressionism, such as light color and visible brushstrokes, but each followed their own path. Cézanne sought structure and solidity; Seurat gave color a scientific basis, with small dots; Gauguin abandoned painting directly from nature in favor of imaginative subjects; and Van Gogh used color and brushwork to express emotion.

Van Gogh's encounter with Impressionism happened in Paris. He moved to the city in February 1886 to live with his brother Theo, an art dealer, and there he saw Impressionist paintings up close, along with the Neo-Impressionism of Seurat and Paul Signac. According to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, during this period he lightened his palette, experimented with the broken brushstrokes of the Impressionists and the pointillist touch of the Neo-Impressionists, and painted more than twenty self-portraits exploring contrasts of complementary colors. In February 1888 he left for Arles, in the south of France, where his color became even more intense and expressive.

cells.text: To capture the light and visual impression of a moment
To go beyond observation: structure, symbol and emotion
It varies: dots in Seurat, built-up planes in Cézanne, bold strokes in Van Gogh
Monet, Renoir, Degas, Morisot, Pissarro, Sisley

children.text: Famous Impressionist works to know
Impression, Sunrise
, Claude Monet, 1872. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris.
Springtime
, Claude Monet, 1872. The Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.
The Cradle
, Berthe Morisot, 1872. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.
Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette
, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1876. Musée d'Orsay, Paris.
Paris Street; Rainy Day
, Gustave Caillebotte, 1877. The Art Institute of Chicago.
The Cliff Walk at Pourville

, Claude Monet, 1882. The Art Institute of Chicago. This is the painting that opens this article: the wind in the grass, the shimmer of the sea and the clouds are built with short brushstrokes and pure colors.
Impressionism as inspiration today
More than 150 years after the first exhibition, Impressionism keeps inspiring people who paint, take photographs or simply like to watch the light. On the
About

page, Mariane Nunes names Monet, Degas and Van Gogh among the references that stay with her, for the way these painters handle movement, light and color. They are inspirations, not membership in a school.
In works such as
Venice at Dusk
and
Path at Dusk
, the late-afternoon light and intense colors take center stage, in a free dialogue with this way of seeing.
The same passion gave rise to two digital planners.
En Plein Air
, whose name refers to painting outdoors, is inspired by Impressionist painting and includes artwork observation pages, with questions and fun facts.
Luminous Days
is inspired by Van Gogh and includes guided encounters with works such as
Irises
Sunflowers
and
Almond Blossom
. To bring this conversation into everyday life, see also
how to use a digital planner
How to look at an Impressionist painting

The best way to understand Impressionism is to look slowly. Choose a work, look closely at the brushstrokes and at the colors that make up the shadows, and then step back a few paces. It is in that back and forth that the painting comes together. And if you want to try the idea on paper, the guide to
oil pastel techniques
shows how to build color with visible strokes.

children.text: Violet Refuge (2025), watercolor on paper.
See the work

Watercolor has a reputation for being difficult, and part of that reputation comes from its greatest charm: water has a will of its own. It spreads color, creates unexpected blooms and hides almost nothing. With the right materials and a few simple exercises, though, that unpredictability stops being scary and becomes part of the fun.

This guide brings together the essentials of watercolor painting for beginners: what to buy, how to prepare the paper, how to balance water and pigment and which techniques to practice first. If you want to know how to paint with watercolor without getting frustrated in your first attempts, start here.
Watercolor is a transparent paint: the light in the painting comes from the white of the paper.
Paper is the most important item in the kit. A 300 gsm paper, preferably with cotton, makes a big difference.
The two basic techniques are wet on wet, for soft edges, and wet on dry, for crisp edges.
In general, you paint from light to dark, in layers, waiting for each one to dry.
How watercolor works

Watercolor paint is made of pigment and a water-soluble binder, traditionally gum arabic. When diluted, it forms thin, transparent layers that let through the light reflected by the paper. That is why, in traditional watercolor, white almost never comes from white paint: it is the paper itself, left unpainted.

This transparency also sets the order of work. You normally paint from light to dark: first the brightest areas and light washes, then the shadows and details. A dark color applied too early is hard to lighten later.
Watercolor materials: the essential kit
You do not need to spend a lot to start, but it helps to know where to invest. If your budget is tight, prioritize the paper.
Paper
Paper is what most affects the result. Thin papers buckle when wet and form puddles where the paint pools. Look at three characteristics:
Weight:

300 gsm, equivalent to 140 lb, is the most common choice. It takes plenty of water, can be stretched so it does not buckle and is moderately priced. Lighter papers, such as those around 190 gsm (90 lb), buckle easily.
Composition:
100% cotton papers absorb water more evenly and handle corrections better. Cellulose papers are cheaper and work well for studies and exercises.
Texture:
it changes how the paint behaves, as the table below shows.

cells.text: Details and fine lines; edges tend to be more pronounced
General use; the most versatile and the best choice to start

children.text: Paints

Watercolor is sold in pans and in tubes. Pans are practical and last a long time; tubes make it easier to prepare large amounts of color at once. There are student and artist ranges: artist paints usually have more pigment and cleaner colors, but a good student set is enough to learn.
A small palette teaches more than a huge box. With a yellow, a red, a blue and an earth tone, you can already mix greens, oranges, purples and grays, and you learn how colors behave together.
Brushes

Two brushes cover almost everything at first: a medium round with a good point, which works for both larger areas and details, and a flat, for broad washes. Synthetic brushes made for watercolor are a great option to start.
Other items
Two jars of water: one to clean the brush and another with clean water to dilute the colors.
A white palette or a ceramic plate, to prepare your mixes.
Paper towels, to remove excess water from the brush and lift color.
Masking tape and a rigid board.
A soft pencil and a clean eraser, for a very light sketch.
How to prepare the paper

Before painting, tape the paper to a board along all four edges with masking tape. This reduces buckling while you paint and, as a bonus, leaves a clean white border when you carefully remove the tape.

Thinner papers can be stretched before use: wet the sheet evenly, fix it to a board with gummed tape and let it dry completely. As it dries, the paper becomes taut and buckles much less. Another option is blocks glued on all four sides, where each sheet stays attached to the block until the painting dries.
Make your sketch with light lines. Graphite stays visible under transparent layers, and an eraser used with force can damage the surface of the paper.
Water and pigment: the watercolor balance
Almost everything in watercolor depends on two questions: how much water is on the brush and how much water is on the paper.
The amount of pigment on the brush

A comparison helps: very diluted, like tea, the mix works for light washes and skies; more concentrated, like milk, for the mid-tones; creamy, with almost no water, for the darks and details. Always test the color on a scrap of paper before applying it, because watercolor dries lighter.
How wet the paper is

As it dries, the paper goes through several stages: soaked, with puddles; damp and shiny; damp but already matte; and dry. The same brushstroke behaves differently in each one. On soaked paper, the color spreads a lot; once it is matte, the paint spreads little and the edges are easier to control.
A classic effect shows this relationship well: when you touch an almost dry area with a brush loaded with water, the water pushes the pigment and forms a stain with jagged edges, known as a bloom or
backrun
. Sometimes it is wanted. Most of the time, it is a sign that it was worth waiting for the area to dry.
Watercolor techniques for beginners
Flat wash

This is an area of even color, like a clear sky. Tilt the board slightly, load the brush well and paint horizontal bands that touch, pulling down the bead of paint that forms at the bottom edge with each new band. Mix enough paint before you start, because stopping halfway leaves marks.
Graded wash

It follows the same logic as the flat wash, but with each band you add a little water to the brush, so the color gradually gets lighter. It is the perfect exercise for skies that darken toward the top.
Wet on wet

First you wet the paper with clean water, or with a color that is still damp, and then you apply the paint. The color spreads and blends by itself, creating soft edges and delicate transitions. It suits skies, backgrounds, clouds and reflections on water. The secret is to control the amount of water and accept that part of the result will be decided by the paint itself.
Wet on dry

The paint is applied on dry paper. The edges stay crisp and the color remains where you put it. This is the technique for details: mountain outlines, branches, windows, people and anything that needs precision.
Layers (glazing)

Once a layer is dry, you can apply another transparent color on top. The two add up visually: a blue over a dry yellow gives a luminous green. Wait for the previous layer to dry completely and avoid scrubbing with the brush, so you do not lift the paint underneath.
Lifting color

With a clean damp brush or a paper towel, you can remove part of the paint while it is still wet and, depending on the pigment and the paper, even once it is dry. The technique is useful for opening clouds in a blue sky, creating reflections or fixing small excesses.
Saving the whites

Since white comes from the paper, plan ahead which areas will stay unpainted: the glint of a window, the foam of a wave, the light on a roof. You can paint around them with the brush or protect them with tape or masking fluid before painting.
Looking at finished watercolors
Looking at finished works helps you recognize these techniques on paper. In the watercolors in the Efúgio Atelier portfolio, a few things to observe:
Violet Refuge
: in the sky, the sunset colors shift from one tone to the next, while the mountain and the house have crisp outlines.
Rio de Janeiro in Watercolor
: the blue of the sea and the bulk of Sugarloaf Mountain contrast with the colorful umbrellas on the sand.
Solitude
: an almost monochrome palette, in grays and olive, shows how few colors are enough to create atmosphere.
Exercises for the first weeks
Color chart.
Paint a small square of each color in your palette, very diluted on one side and concentrated on the other. You will get to know the intensity and transparency of each paint.
Value scale.
With a single color, paint five squares, from lightest to darkest. The exercise trains your control of the ratio between water and pigment.
Washes.
Fill rectangles with flat washes and graded washes until you get results without marks.
Wet on wet.
Wet a circle on the paper and drop in two neighboring colors, such as blue and yellow. Watch how they mix without your help.
A landscape in three stages.
Paint a sky wet on wet. Once it is dry, add a band of mountains wet on dry and, finally, the foreground details. It sums up everything you have practiced.
Common watercolor mistakes
Too little paint and too much water.
The result looks pale once dry. Remember that watercolor dries lighter.
Overworking.
Going back to the same area again and again takes the freshness out of the painting and can wear down the paper. Apply, observe and let it dry.
Not waiting for it to dry.
Layers applied over areas that are still damp mix and form unwanted stains.
Mixing too many colors.
Three or more colors in the same mix usually turn into a grayish or muddy tone.
Using thin paper.
Many beginner frustrations are actually the paper's fault.
Forgetting the whites.
Once painted, light areas are hard to recover.
Start small, but start

Watercolor is learned through repetition: small paintings made often teach more than a big piece that never leaves the drawing board. Set aside a good sheet and a short palette and practice the exercises in this guide one at a time.
To get to know a material with a very different logic, more direct and full-bodied, read the guide to
oil pastel
. And to understand why light became so important in painting, it is worth learning
what Impressionism is

keywords.keyword: how to paint with oil pastels

children.text: Venice at Dusk (2025), oil pastel on paper.
See the work

Oil pastel is one of those materials that look simple in the box and surprise you on paper. With a single stick you can cover an area with intense color, blend two tones with a fingertip or scrape away a layer to reveal the color underneath. Since it needs no brush, no water and no drying time, it is often a great way in for anyone who wants to start painting.

This guide explains what oil pastel is, how it differs from other pastels, which materials to choose and how to paint with oil pastels step by step, from the first layers to the techniques that bring texture and light to a painting.
Oil pastel is made of pigment bound with wax and a non-drying oil. That is why it has vivid color, a creamy texture and almost no dust.
To start, all you need is a box of pastels, a heavyweight paper and a few simple accessories, such as a blending stump and paper towels.
The basic techniques are layering, color blending, hatching, sgraffito and impasto.
Because oil pastel never hardens completely, a finished piece needs protection, ideally a mat and glass.
What oil pastel is

Oil pastel is a stick of color made of pigment mixed with wax and a non-drying oil. This combination gives the material a consistency somewhere between a wax crayon and oil paint: it glides over the paper, covers well, blends and lets you build thick layers with visible texture.

Another important trait is that oil pastel does not dry the way paint does. Over time the surface becomes firmer to the touch, but it stays a little soft and delicate. This lets you rework an area days later, and it explains why a finished piece needs care when it is stored.
A 20th-century invention

Unlike watercolor or oil paint, which have centuries of history, oil pastel is a recent material. In 1925 the Japanese company Sakura launched Cray-Pas, which the manufacturer itself presents as the world's first oil pastel. It was created so that children could express themselves with more freedom and color in art class.

The version made for artists came in the late 1940s. According to Sennelier, the Paris art supply house, Pablo Picasso asked Henri Sennelier for a color that could be used on almost any surface, such as wood, cardboard, metal and paper. After about a year of research, the result was a very oily stick of wax and pigment, with strong adhesion, that never fully hardens.
Oil pastel, soft pastel and wax crayon: what is the difference
The three sit side by side in art supply stores, but they behave very differently on paper.

cells.text: Pigment with wax and a non-drying oil
Pigment with little binder, such as gum
Easy, with a finger, a blending stump or by layering colors
Never fully dries; protect it with a mat and glass
Fragile; usually gets fixative and glass

children.text: In practice, oil pastel sits in the middle: it has the color strength of soft pastel without the dust, and the ease of a wax crayon, with many more possibilities for blending and texture.
Materials for oil pastel
One of the advantages of oil pastel is that the starter kit is small. These are the items that make a difference from the very first painting.
The pastels

There are student ranges and artist ranges. Student pastels are firmer and cheaper, great for experimenting. Artist pastels usually have more pigment, more intense colors and a softer texture, which makes blending and layering easier. To start, a box of about 24 colors already offers enough variety. More important than the number of colors is having good light tones, especially white, which you will use a lot to lighten and bring colors together.
Paper and other surfaces

Oil pastel adheres best to surfaces with a little texture, the so-called "tooth" of the paper, which holds the pigment. Thin, smooth papers saturate quickly, wrinkle with friction and cannot take many layers. Choose:
papers made for pastel
, with a texture designed to hold pigment;
heavyweight drawing or watercolor papers
colored or toned papers
, which act as a mid-tone and help you build light and shadow faster.
Since the material was designed to adhere to many surfaces, you can also paint on board, wood or primed canvas. For your first paintings, though, a heavyweight paper is the simplest choice.
Helpful accessories
A blending stump or cotton swab
, to blend colors without getting your fingers greasy.
Paper towels or a cloth
, to clean the tips of the pastels, which pick up color from the layers underneath.
A wooden stick or small palette knife
, to scrape layers in the sgraffito technique.
Masking tape and a drawing board
, to hold the paper in place and keep a clean margin.
Odorless solvent (optional)
, to dissolve the pastel and create wash effects. Use a small amount, in a ventilated space, following the manufacturer's instructions.
How to use oil pastels: step by step
There is no single order, but this sequence works well for first paintings and helps you avoid the most common beginner mistake: saturating the paper too early.
Make a light sketch.
Mark only the main shapes with a light pencil or with the pastel itself, in a tone close to that of the area you will paint. Dark graphite lines can mix with the color and muddy the result.
Cover the large areas with little pressure.
Start with the background and the largest masses of color, such as sky, sea or field, passing the pastel lightly. This first layer still lets the tooth of the paper show.
Build up the layers.
Add colors gradually, increasing the pressure. This is the stage where blends, shadows and the sense of volume appear.
Blend wherever you want smooth transitions.
Use a finger, a blending stump or a light tone applied on top to merge two colors.
Leave details and highlights for last.
The lightest, most intense touches, such as a glint on water or the reflection on a piece of fruit, go on last, with more pressure. Good-quality pastels usually cover well even over dark colors.
Oil pastel techniques
These are the most widely used techniques in oil pastel painting. It is worth testing each one on a scrap of paper before taking it into a finished piece.
Layering

Applying color over color is the basis of everything. Start with light pressure and increase it gradually. If the first layers are too heavy, the paper saturates, the pastel starts to slide without sticking and the top color drags the one below. With thin layers, you can stack several tones and reach richer colors.
Color blending
There are three main ways to blend:
By layering:
apply one color and then another on top, rubbing with the pastel itself. The lighter tone usually works best as the top layer.
With tools:
rub with a finger, a blending stump or a cotton swab to merge the colors and soften the edges.
With white:
passing white or a very light tone over two neighboring colors helps join them and creates delicate transitions, great for skies.

One important caution: overblending, or blending colors that sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, tends to make the result grayish. Often, leaving two pure colors side by side, unblended, gives the painting more vibrancy.
Hatching and optical mixing

Instead of blending the colors, you can apply them in short strokes, parallel or crossed, and let the eye do the mixing from a distance. Building color with visible marks is an idea closely tied to Impressionist painting, the subject of the guide
what Impressionism is
Sgraffito

Apply a layer of color and cover it with another, darker or contrasting one. Then scrape the top layer with a wooden stick or a palette knife to reveal the color underneath. The technique is great for drawing branches, blades of grass, wood grain and other fine details that are hard to make with the thick tip of the pastel.
Impasto

With strong pressure and several layers, oil pastel forms a thick surface with relief, similar to that of an oil painting. This build-up of material gives weight to fruit, flowers and reflections of light. In the painting
Lemons
, for example, oil pastel makes the skin of the fruit look almost raised.
Solvent wash

When you pass a brush or cotton swab lightly dampened with solvent over the pastel, the color dissolves and spreads like thin paint. The effect is useful for filling backgrounds and creating very soft transitions. Since it involves chemicals, it is an optional technique: use little product, keep the space ventilated and follow the manufacturer's guidance.
Examples from the portfolio
A few works in the Efúgio Atelier portfolio help show what oil pastel does best: intense colors, strong contrasts and visible texture.
Rainy Day
: the yellow of the raincoat stands out against the gray of the sea, and the texture of the pastel marks the waves.
Path at Dusk
: green fields, blue mountains and an orange sky in pure colors.
Feline Gaze
: the intense green of the leaves frames the cat's spotted coat.
Common beginner mistakes
Pressing too hard right away.
The paper saturates and the next layers do not stick. Start light and leave strong pressure for the end.
Using thin paper.
It wrinkles, tears with friction and cannot hold several layers.
Not cleaning the pastels.
The tip picks up the color underneath and starts to smudge the light areas. A paper towel nearby solves it.
Blending everything.
Merging every color takes the vibrancy out of the painting and can make the tones grayish.
Starting with the details.
Work from the large masses of color to the details, not the other way around.
Forgetting to protect the artwork.
Since oil pastel never fully dries, the surface can smudge or stick to another sheet.
How to store and protect an oil pastel painting

Because the material stays slightly soft, the safest way to display an oil pastel painting is to frame it with a mat and glass. The mat creates a gap between the glass and the painting and keeps the surface from touching it and sticking. To store unframed work, interleave the sheets with glassine or parchment paper and keep them flat, away from heat.
There are also fixatives made specifically for oil pastel, which help protect the surface. If you use one, check the manufacturer's recommendations and test it on a study first.
To start today

Oil pastel rewards curiosity. Choose a simple subject, such as a piece of fruit, a sunset or a landscape with few elements, set aside a heavyweight paper and try the techniques in this guide one at a time. Within a few paintings you will notice how the pressure of your hand, the order of the layers and the choice of colors completely change the result.
If you also want to explore the transparency and lightness of water, read the guide to
watercolor painting for beginners
. And to see the material in finished works, visit the
oil pastel paintings in the portfolio
